Laboratory studies on the slipper limpet Crepidula fornicata have provided detailed insights into its early life history. At a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], hatching from the egg capsule occurs approximately 27 days [ab = approximately 27 days] after oviposition, a developmental period that aligns with the protracted embryogenesis observed in other calyptraeid gastropods. Newly hatched individuals emerge as planktotrophic veliger larvae with a prodissoconch shell length at birth of 0.046 cm [Lb = 0.046 cm], a modest size that reflects the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. The duration of this embryonic phase appears tightly coupled to thermal conditions, as metabolic rates in poikilotherms are strongly temperature-dependent. Upon release, these microscopic larvae begin cilia-driven feeding on phytoplankton, initiating a phase of rapid growth and morphological differentiation that will culminate in metamorphosis and settlement onto the substrate.

The interval between hatching and the attainment of metamorphic competence has been precisely characterized under controlled conditions. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is 31 days since birth , during which the veliger larva grows and develops a functional foot and a well-defined velum. This pelagic period is critical for dispersal, yet it also exposes the larva to substantial planktonic predation risk. At the point of metamorphic competence, the shell length at metamorphosis is 0.097 cm , representing nearly a doubling of size relative to the birth length. The growth rate at this stage, measured specifically at the shell length corresponding to metamorphic competence, reaches 0.01105 cm per day  under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Once the larva encounters a suitable substratum, it undergoes a rapid metamorphic climax involving velum loss, gill development, and the transition to a benthic juvenile existence.

Following settlement and metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a period of rapid somatic growth and reproductive development. Field data indicate that the shell length at the onset of male puberty is 0.4 cm [Lp = 0.4 cm], a size threshold at which functional male gametogenesis is initiated. Under the standard laboratory temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at puberty for male function is 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth], as interpolated from length-at-age growth curves. This relatively rapid maturation of the male function is characteristic of the protandrous hermaphroditic life history that defines Crepidula fornicata, in which individuals initially mature as males and later transition to the female sex at a larger size. The functional significance of this sequential hermaphroditism is often interpreted in terms of size-advantage models, which posit that male reproductive success benefits less from large body size than does female fecundity.

Reproductive output in Crepidula fornicata has been quantified from observations of brooding females maintained under stable thermal conditions. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a sexually mature female produces approximately 30 eggs per brood capsule [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per brood capsule], with females typically depositing approximately 365 brood capsules per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 brood capsules per year]. This high fecundity is sustained by the species' filter-feeding lifestyle, which allows continuous energy intake. The maximum ingestion rate under these conditions is 500,000,000 cells of Phaeodactylum tricornutum per day per gram of wet weight , reflecting an impressive capacity for exploiting dense phytoplankton blooms at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This energetic subsidy underpins the species' invasive success, as high feeding rates support both rapid somatic growth and continuous gamete production across a protracted breeding season spanning much of the year in temperate waters.

Long-term observations of marked individuals in the field reveal that Crepidula fornicata exhibits a remarkable maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 5 years [am = 5 years] of age at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a gastropod of its adult body size and contributes to the species' ability to form dense, multi-cohort aggregations on hard substrata. The ultimate shell length, representing the maximum attainable size in undisturbed populations, is 5.3 cm [Li = 5.3 cm], though mean adult size is often somewhat smaller due to density-dependent competition for space and food within these stacks. Comparative studies with congeners such as Crepidula convexa, which rarely exceeds 2.5 cm in shell length, underscore the relatively large body size attained by Crepidula fornicata. This combination of high feeding rates, early male maturation, protandrous sex change, and extended lifespan collectively defines a life-history strategy that has proven extraordinarily successful in colonizing temperate coastlines worldwide.
